clinicalPearls: A rare autosomal dominant bleeding disorder characterised by delayed-onset bleeding after trauma or surgery, often hours to a day later
Bleeding is typically responsive to antifibrinolytic therapy but not to platelet transfusion, a distinctive and clinically important feature
The platelet count is usually normal or only mildly reduced, so it is a qualitative defect
The underlying lesion is a tandem duplication of the PLAU gene, causing marked overexpression of urokinase-type plasminogen activator within megakaryocytes and platelets
Excess intraplatelet urokinase drives premature plasmin generation and proteolytic degradation of alpha-granule proteins
It can be mistaken for an alpha-granule storage pool defect because of the secondary loss of granule contents
Recognition matters because antifibrinolytic cover, rather than platelet transfusion, is the effective haemostatic strategy
reference.pathophysiology: Quebec platelet disorder is caused by a tandem duplication of PLAU, the gene encoding urokinase-type plasminogen activator. Overexpression of urokinase within developing megakaryocytes leads to accumulation of the enzyme in platelet alpha granules, where it generates plasmin intracellularly. This premature, localised plasmin activity degrades stored alpha-granule proteins such as factor V, fibrinogen, von Willebrand factor, and others. The net effect is an intraplatelet hyperfibrinolytic state that undermines clot stability at sites of injury, producing characteristically delayed bleeding despite a relatively preserved platelet count.
additionalDifferentials: Platelet alpha-granule storage pool deficiency (including gray platelet syndrome)
Alpha-2-antiplasmin deficiency and other hyperfibrinolytic bleeding states
additionalInvestigations: Detailed bleeding history emphasising delayed post-traumatic or postoperative bleeding
Platelet aggregation studies, which may show a reduced response to certain agonists
Assay or immunoblot demonstrating increased platelet urokinase-type plasminogen activator
Measurement of reduced platelet alpha-granule protein content
Genetic testing for the PLAU tandem duplication to confirm the diagnosis
Von Willebrand factor and coagulation factor assays to exclude alternative disorders
redFlags: Severe delayed bleeding after surgery, trauma, or dental extraction
Bleeding that fails to respond to platelet transfusion
Joint or deep-tissue bleeding suggesting a significant haemostatic defect
Unrecognised diagnosis leading to inappropriate transfusion before an invasive procedure
reference.prognosis: With correct diagnosis and antifibrinolytic cover around haemostatic challenges, most patients do well and lead normal lives. Failure to recognise the disorder can lead to preventable, sometimes serious, delayed haemorrhage.
pitfalls: Relying on platelet transfusion, which is ineffective, rather than antifibrinolytic therapy
Misclassifying it as a simple alpha-granule storage pool defect
Being reassured by a normal platelet count and near-normal routine coagulation screen
Underestimating risk because bleeding is delayed rather than immediate
references: Hoffman: Hematology - Basic Principles and Practice
